task_text: Goal: estimate a classifier's performance on NEW patients. Each patient has five highly correlated visits. Which pipelines are valid estimates of this goal? A: random visit split, train-only scaling, tune only on train. B: patient-group train/validation/test split, train-only fit of preprocessing and model, tune on validation, locked test once. C: patient-group split but supervised feature selection on all labels before splitting. D: patient-group split, fit on train but use test results to choose best of 20 variants and report that test. E: nested patient-group CV, preprocessing/selection/tuning all inside each outer training fold, evaluate each outer test once, no post-hoc variant choice. F: train on visits before June and test on later visits from the SAME patients. Return valid_pipeline_ids as a list, A_issue/C_issue/D_issue/F_issue chosen from patient_overlap, supervised_leakage, test_selection_bias, temporal_drift_only, none. Conditional on one visit in test in an independent 80% train /20% test visit split, return probability_patient_also_in_train using its other four visits. Is a reported increase after choosing the best of 20 test-set variants alone evidence of a genuine improvement? Return genuine_improvement_established (boolean).

response.concise_method_summary: The goal is generalization to unseen patients, so any valid pipeline must keep all visits from a given patient entirely within one split (patient-grouping) and must never let test/validation information influence preprocessing, feature selection, or model choice. A fails because a random visit-level split puts correlated visits from the same patient in both train and test. C fails because supervised feature selection uses labels from the full dataset (including future test patients) before splitting. D fails because repeatedly consulting test performance to pick among 20 variants turns the test set into a tuning set, inflating the reported number. F fails because, despite a temporal cut, the same patients appear in both train and test, so patient-specific correlation leaks across the split regardless of the time boundary. B and E are valid: B uses a single patient-grouped train/val/test split with train-only fitting and one locked test evaluation; E uses nested patient-grouped cross-validation with all preprocessing/selection/tuning confined to each outer training fold and a single outer-test evaluation, with no post-hoc variant selection. For the conditional-probability question: in an independent 80%/20% per-visit split, each of a patient's other four visits is included in train independently with probability 0.8, so the probability that at least one of the other four visits lands in train, given one visit is in test, is 1 − 0.2^4 = 1 − 0.0016 = 0.9984. Finally, choosing the best of 20 variants using test-set results alone is a form of test-set overfitting (multiple comparisons/selection bias): the observed 'improvement' is expected under pure noise and is not evidence of genuine improvement without an independent confirmation set.
assumptions: F_issue is scored as patient_overlap rather than temporal_drift_only because the same patients appear on both sides of the time cut, so patient-specific correlation contaminates the estimate independent of any drift effect
The 80%/20% split referenced in the probability question is an independent per-visit (visit-level) Bernoulli assignment, not a patient-grouped split
Each patient contributes exactly five visits and visit inclusion/exclusion events are independent across visits
'Train-only scaling' in A does not fix the core issue because the split itself already mixes a patient's visits across train and test
No additional information leakage mechanisms (e.g., shared IDs, timestamps as features) are assumed beyond what is stated
proposed_verification: Empirically compare AUC/accuracy under a random visit-level split (A) vs. a patient-grouped split (B) on the same data; a large gap confirms leakage inflation
Re-run D but with a third, never-touched holdout set evaluated once after variant selection on the original test set, and compare the two numbers to quantify test-set selection bias
Simulate the independent 80/20 per-visit split many times and empirically estimate P(patient also in train | one visit in test) to confirm it matches 1 − 0.2^4
For F, rerun with patients (not just time) split into disjoint train/test groups and compare performance drop, isolating drift from patient-overlap leakage
For E, verify no information (scaling stats, selected features, hyperparameters) computed on an outer test fold was used anywhere in that fold's training pipeline
Apply a permutation/label-shuffle test to the 'best of 20' improvement in D to check whether a comparable gain arises by chance alone
